content: Leptospirosis is an infectious disease caused by bacteria. These bacteria are primarily spread through the urine of infected animals. When an infected animal urinates, the bacteria can contaminate water or soil, where they can survive for weeks to months. Humans can become infected by coming into contact with fresh water, soil, or objects that have been contaminated with the urine of infected animals. The most common routes of infection include the bacteria entering the body through the eyes, nose, mouth, or broken skin, such as cuts or scratches. Additionally, consuming food or water that has been contaminated can also lead to infection. Some individuals infected with leptospirosis may not exhibit any symptoms. However, when symptoms do occur, they can include fever, headache, chills, muscle aches, vomiting, jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes), red eyes, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and occasionally a rash. If left untreated, leptospirosis can lead to severe complications, such as kidney damage, liver failure, or meningitis (inflammation of the lining of the brain and spinal cord). In some cases, the disease can be fatal. Treatment with antibiotics is essential to prevent these serious outcomes. Leptospirosis is found worldwide but is most prevalent in regions with temperate or tropical climates. These areas include South and Southeast Asia, Oceania, the Caribbean, parts of sub-Saharan Africa, and parts of Latin America. Travelers are at an increased risk of contracting leptospirosis if they engage in certain activities, such as visiting areas that have been recently flooded, swimming, wading, kayaking, or rafting in potentially contaminated freshwater sources like lakes and rivers, visiting urban areas with poor sanitation, or coming into contact with animals or their bodily fluids. Animals that can carry the bacteria include rodents, cows, sheep, goats, pigs, horses, dogs, and various wildlife species. Currently, there is no vaccine available in the United States to prevent leptospirosis in humans. Travelers can take several precautions to reduce their risk of infection. These include avoiding contact with fresh water or soil that may be contaminated with animal urine, avoiding contact with objects that could be contaminated, such as animal bedding, and refraining from wading, swimming, or submerging their head in floodwaters or freshwater sources, especially after heavy rains or flooding. For some individuals, taking prophylactic medication before traveling to high-risk areas may be an option. Travelers should consult their healthcare provider before their trip to discuss their planned activities and determine whether preventive medication is appropriate.
